Jim Robb Opening Statement
FERC Reliability Technical Conference
October 21, 2026

Good morning, Chairman and Commissioners. Always an honor to help set the table at this
annual engagement. I especially appreciate you including Jeff Droubay, the CEO of WECC, one
of the 6 Regional Entities we work with, on the second panel.

I’ll ﬁrst review the context of reliability risk then turn to our work supporting reliable integration
of computational load.

BPS reliability remains a paradox. By most objective measures, the BPS remains extraordinarily
reliable; however near-miss events and signiﬁcant new and intensifying risks challenge the
ability to sustain that performance. Top risks include:

   • Reduced resource adequacy that risks energy shortage in many areas of the Continent

   • Unprecedented load growth which further challenges resource adequacy

   •    A shift to power electronic-based generation and load that bring unique performance
       challenges and can create and/or amplify grid disturbances

   • Extreme weather that impacts not only load, but also delivery infrastructure and the
     ability to generate power

   • Policies that frustrate the pace of energy infrastructure development

   • And persistent cyber and physical security threats growing in sophistication and
     ampliﬁed by AI and the prospect of quantum computing

These risks result in a system that is running ever closer to the edge and increasingly reliant
upon extraordinary operator actions with little room for error. While recent policy and
industry actions are helping to mitigate these risks, the overall situation remains highly
concerning and continues to merit a “ﬁve alarm ﬁre” response.




RELIABILITY | RESILIENCE | SECURITY

POWERING TODAY. PROTECTING TOMORROW.
 Last year’s Long-Term Reliability Assessment found more than half of the Continent faces
resource adequacy challenges over the next 10 years:

   • The LTRA projected summer demand would rise by nearly 225 GW and winter demand
     by nearly 250 GW, driven by data centers, industrial expansion, population migration
     and electriﬁcation policies

   • Projected generation and transmission development is not expected to keep up with
     that load growth and planned generation often does not show up when anticipated
     due to siting, permitting, or supply chain challenges.

   • Most new resources expected to come online in the next ﬁve years consist of battery
     storage and solar photovoltaic. While these resources can make important
     contributions in some markets, they struggle to make meaningful reliability
     contributions in others, especially in winter.

   • Signiﬁcant conventional generator retirements loom in the next ﬁve years, reducing the
     amount of generation with onsite fuel and impacting the system’s ability to respond to
     changing conditions. These retirements have also exposed signiﬁcant vulnerabilities
     related to the natural gas system, which now provides nearly half of the fuel for power
     generation in the country.

   • And, within the remaining conventional ﬂeet, we are seeing a meaningful increase in
     forced outage rates.

The recent review of last winter’s arctic systems underscores these dynamics requiring
system operators to rely on their full toolbox to keep the lights on. We observed similar
issues during this past summer’s heat domes. Despite emergency orders from the Secretary
of Energy, increasing numbers of energy emergencies have been called. These actions should
not be normalized – there is clearly more work to be done.

We see four major areas needing attention to ameliorate this situation:




FERC Reliability Technical Conference – October 21, 2026   2
   1) First, better forecasting of supply and demand is needed to strengthen planning and
     operational readiness as well as policy maker understanding of risk:

      • Our work on developing an energy assurance standard aims to improve
        understanding of how much dependable energy is available to serve load during
        periods of stress.

      • And, we are enhancing our assessments to include expanded energy demand
        forecasts, better assessments of anticipated energy availability, and the availability
        of inter-regional transfers.

  2) Generation and transmission additions are urgently needed.

      • We applaud the Commission for pursuing nationwide interconnection reforms,
        changes to transmission planning and permitting programs, and approving fast-track
        programs by the RTOs and ISOs.

      • These expedited programs are critically important, however more progress is needed
        to reduce barriers that frustrate timely resource development. As the sensitivity
        study we conducted last year on MISO’s ERAS program highlighted, simply being
        studied doesn’t translate directly to machines spitting out kwhs

  3) Continued progress is needed to support reliable integration of IBRs:

      • Last year we updated our Compliance Registry to include smaller IBR entities,
        closing a critical reliability gap driven by common mode failure risk.

      • We recently completed our work to address FERC Order 901 regarding Reliability
        Standards for IBRs, addressing gaps in disturbance performance, monitoring, data
        sharing, and modeling.




FERC Reliability Technical Conference – October 21, 2026   3
       • But we shouldn’t declare victory yet: our studies of international events, such as the
        Iberian outage of 2025, point to additional work that will likely need to be
        undertaken to create a reliable and resilient system integrating large amounts of
        IBRs and DERs.

   4) We at NERC will also continue to modernize our processes and strategies for the
      contemporary risk environment:

      • We are making strong progress to modernize our Standards Development Process to
        better keep up with the speed of risk.

      • We are enhancing our reliability assessments through wide area energy demand
        forecasting, inter-regional transmission analysis, and improved categorization of
        generator additions/retirements.

      • Our Electric Power-Natural Gas Coordination Strategy includes new data collection
        to better assess natural gas supply risks.

      • We are implementing our Wildfire Mitigation workplan to reduce risk within our
        authority and engage industry and governments in areas beyond.

      • And the E-ISAC continues to work with industry on mitigating complex, ever-
        evolving threats. The ISAC is currently hosting our annual grid security conference
        and we are in the depth of planning the next GridEx tabletop to be held next
        February exercise.

I’ll spend the balance of my time on NERC’s work enabling reliable integration of
computational load; this is a high-priority objective that is critical to the bulk power system,
as well as US competitiveness and national security.

The rapid growth of data centers, artificial intelligence, crypto-mining, and other large
computational loads creates challenges well beyond resource adequacy. These facilities can
change consumption quickly or disconnect together during a disturbance, creating risks that
planners and operators must understand and manage.




FERC Reliability Technical Conference – October 21, 2026   4
 I am incredibly proud of the pace at which the NERC team and industry is executing to
address this rapidly escalating risk. Let me summarize three of our key actions:

      1) We are taking action based on two recently formed industry SME groups:

              a. Based on the Large Loads Working Group’s technical analysis, we issued a
                 Reliability guideline and an Essential Action Alert last May as well as a road
                 map for future risk mitigation actions.

              b. Based on the Load Modeling Working Groups analysis, we issued a data
                 center modeling reference guide to give utilities, facility owners, and
                 equipment manufacturers a common foundation for better modeling of
                 these unique loads.

      2) Last week, NERC’s Board of Trustees approved registry criteria for computational
         loads, along with two new functional entity types. Congress had the foresight to
         envision reliability risk from users of the BPS; this represents a historic moment in
         the application that authority.

          This action recognizes that computational load behavior can affect the wider grid
          and that they must share reliability accountability as good citizens of the grid. We
          will file the registration criteria with the Commission later this week

      3) Finally, the proposed foundational standards for commissioning computational
         loads recently passed their initial and final ballots by a wide margin. This is a
         remarkable accomplishment for a “clean sheet” standard.

          These Standards address three basic needs:

          • First, utilities will have sound interconnection studies and reliable models.
            Computational load owners will provide facility information, verify that models
            reflect installed equipment and settings, and coordinate commissioning while
            planners and operators will understand how and when a facility might
            disconnect, remain connected, or reconnect

          • Second, grid operators will receive timely operating information and clear
            communications. Computational load operators will maintain direct


FERC Reliability Technical Conference – October 21, 2026   5
               communications, train personnel to receive instructions, and follow those
              instructions within specified safety, equipment, and legal limitations.

          • A third standard requires coordination of protection settings and recording
            capabilities for breaker operations, faults, and dynamic disturbances. These
            synchronized measurements will help event investigators determine what
            happened and assess facility performance.

We will present these requirements to the NERC Board of Trustees next Monday for
acceptance and file them with the Commission in early November, well ahead of the deadline
you directed last July.

Work will continue in 2027 to address priority needs including ride-through requirements,
event reporting, root cause analysis, model validation, and the needed security parameters
for these facilities.

                                                           * * *

So there is no shortage of activity as we work apace on numerous fronts simultaneously on
large loads and many other priorities. It goes without saying we appreciate last week’s
Commission Order approving our 2027 Business Plan and Budget to ensure we have the
resources we need to support the reliability and security needs of this unprecedented risk
environment. Thank you, and I look forward to the discussion.




FERC Reliability Technical Conference – October 21, 2026   6
